en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Danxia Zhen:
In our school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. Yet, within this state of no-dharma, the system of the Five Ranks and Three Mysteries is established;
and within this state of no-words, the discourse of reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs is composed. Like the crashing of thunder...
Like a flash of lightning, neither Māra nor externalists can peer into it; like surging seas and gathering clouds, even the Dragon Palace cannot conceal it.
Yet, he never once began by traversing the lips and tongue to establish written words. Capable of possessing such a mechanism, he loudly proclaimed the Dharma of the Five Ranks of Ruler and Subject.
Whether speaking horizontally or vertically, he was like rolling a round stone from atop a thousand-fathom cliff, leaving no trace behind—this was Danxia.

This refers to Chan Master Chun. His distant descendant, Liangji, fearing that his master’s recorded sayings might be lost over time, has compared and corrected them according to the original texts to produce this new edition.
He has had it carved into woodblocks so that it may circulate forever, and thus requested a preface from me.
I have not declined on account of my lack of literary skill, but have recorded this with care to place it at the beginning of the volume.
It is my hope that future students will possess the discerning eye to examine it closely, and by no means seek understanding through mere words and letters.
Written with reverent prostrations by Wanshan (Zuyuan) on the latter part of the third day of the first month in the year of Gengyin,
the Baoying era. Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Danxia Zhiyun.
Volume One:
Preface;
Dharma Discourses from the High Seat at Mount Dahong; True Eulogies and Verses of Praise.
Volume II, Supplementary Collection:
Discourses from the Upper Hall, Verses on Ancient Cases, and Verses on Ancient Masters;
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chun of Da Hong Mountain in Suizhou.

The junior Dharma heir Qingyu, proofreader for the Master, received the invitation from Da Hong in Suizhou while at Huizhao Hermitage on Mount Dacheng in Tangzhou on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Zhenghe era.
He held up the commentary and said: "Do you understand? Before the pearl of the black dragon is split open, its value is difficult to appraise."
"Blazing with cold light, it reflects upon the azure stream; The formless void cannot know its place of departure. Please rely on further detail to explain the underlying cause.

Having finished reading the memorial, the Master ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "How excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners! In this desolate thatched hut, weeds grow in wild disorder;
At midday, the wooden gate still remains reluctant to open. I sit alone in profound stillness upon a withered root— Who would say that such extraordinary grace is a mere cloud?"
The outsider has arrived; thus, the golden rooster is placed to herald the dawn, once more illuminating the profound mystery of Mount Shaoshi.

The stone maiden sings and dances, chanting anew the wondrous melody of Xinfeng. Truly, a thousand mountains embrace auspicious signs and ten thousand plants manifest blessings; in the eight directions, the Way prospers and the times are peaceful;
throughout the land, the rivers clear and the seas are calm. Do you all understand? It is precisely at this moment, when the chrysanthemums bloom amidst the frosty night.
Furthermore, it was the time when the *pán-táo* (peaches of immortality) bore fruit.
Entering the monastery, he ascended the hall and said: "Rugged peaks stand serene within this ancient Chan temple; Taking a leisurely step, I return once more to a realm of boundless delight.
The wind sweeps away the white clouds, leaving the celestial realm pure; A single red sun hangs precisely in the midst of the sky."

On that day, the administrative official requested a *xiaochan* (small-scale sermon), saying: "The silver altar burns phoenix-tailed candles; their flames illuminate the empty hall. The jeweled pavilion strikes the golden bell;
its sound resonates through the realm of space. Thus, the light of wisdom interpenetrates without interval the wondrous mind of the Buddhas of the past.

The elegant and sacred chanting thunders forth, secretly conveying the secret intent of the Patriarchs. As long as consciousness and emotion are not exhausted, everything one looks upon is erroneous. Roots and objects..."
Suddenly forgetting the divergent paths, one realizes they lead to a single goal. If you can do this, only then will you understand how to cast off the horns and don the fur.
Even so, Daohong’s staff is still not yet willing to grant its approval. I dare ask you all: tell me, what special quality does this staff possess?
After a long silence, he said: "Heaven ordained it to be born upon a thousand peaks; its firm and secret roots remain undiminished in their power."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The morning breeze scatters the azure clouds from the heavens; as the sun rises into the vast sky, the scenery unfolds.
Still illumination contains the void, with neither interior nor exterior. How can one speak of a single phrase? Therefore it is said:
'One phrase should be clarified, not illuminated'; 'one phrase should be illuminated, not clarified'; 'one phrase blends clarity and darkness'; 'one phrase..."
Not falling into light or darkness—among these four propositions, tell me, which one is the guest and which one is the host?
If you can understand this thoroughly, then your journey as a pilgrim is complete. If it is not yet so, then:
"The moon in the empty realm of the ten-thousand-year-old green pool—only after repeated scooping and stirring will you finally know."
Winter Night Small Sermon. Well done, all you practitioners of Chan! Though the golden bell resonates, the stars and moon have not yet been distinguished.

We rely on lamps and candles for illumination and depend on the sensory object of sound to perform the Buddha-work. Thus, the brilliant lights reflect one another and the melodic tones harmonize, transcending ordinary sight and hearing and far surpassing sound and form.
Therefore it is said: "If you wish to know the path of liberation, the various dharmas do not reach one another. The eye—
The ears are cut off from hearing and seeing; sounds and forms are a vast, tumultuous clamor.

If you can thoroughly comprehend this, it may be said that you are like a dragon gaining the water or a tiger taking refuge in the mountains. If this is not yet the case, you will inevitably be spun around by others.
Tonight, Da Hong will not spare his eyebrows as he explains this through for all of you: when the ear-element hears, the eye-element penetrates; one faculty [is the same as all].
Returning to the six spheres, they are perfectly interfused. If you wish to know the luminous ground of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it lies subtly within sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.

On the occasion of the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall and said: "This winter on the mountain, there has been little frost or snow; the weather is bright and mild, like that of the spring months.

On this day, we rejoice that the first yang has arisen, and the plum roots have already begun to sprout. "If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, contemplate it closely at this very moment."
The Winter Solstice. It is precisely at this time that the forests are withered and sparse, and heaven and earth are bitterly cold.
Tell me, from what place does the first yang arise? Do you all understand? If you wish to know where the yang energy secretly emerges, look directly down to the adamantine limit (*vajra-koti*).
If this is not yet so, the auspicious season has already passed. I pray that you may enjoy ten thousand blessings in your daily life.

Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: Counting on my fingers, I joyfully encounter the eighth day of the twelfth month; this is the very hour when Śākyamuni attained enlightenment.
Two thousand years later, I follow in his footsteps and once again bathe my pure body with fragrant water. All you virtuous practitioners of Chan:

In antiquity, there were sixteen noble beings who, while following the custom of entering the bathhouse during a communal bathing, suddenly awakened to the cause of water and clearly realized its wondrous touch, thereby fully entering the Perfect [Enlightenment].
The realm of penetration. Today, Da Hong has issued a general summons for everyone to go to Lingji Hall to perform the ritual bathing of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Within this, there is also a message for those who have attained awakening. Do you all understand? Three or two ladles of fragrant water overflowing and shimmering.
He then poured it over the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
Small Evening Sermon for the Eve of the New Year: Tonight, the year comes to its end; tomorrow, at dawn, we shall welcome the spring.
Time passes with such suddenness that it spares no one; our teeth and hair grow frail as yet another year is added. O Assembly, time flows on and changes; every thought-moment is impermanent.
Time does not wait for man; how could life endure long? Everyone knows that today is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, yet have you ever prepared for what must be done on this day?
Do not treat this as a matter of indifference; you must prepare with the utmost urgency.
But tell me, how do you prepare? Is it by amassing wealth and goods that you prepare?
Is it not preparation by reading and examining the scriptures? Is it not preparation by reciting the *Chan Ce* (Zen manuals)?
Is it not preparation by maintaining a clever and artful mind? At such a moment, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one’s hands and feet will be in a state of frantic confusion.
I remember that once in the past, I forgot for a time. Upon arriving here, you must tread upon solid ground;
you cannot succeed by seeking empty verbiage. Everyone, during your daily activities, you must quickly find rest.
Prepare for departure. Let go of all present concerns. Sit coldly within the Hall of the Withered Tree. You must truly die once over. Then...
Established from the midst of death, you cannot be deceived anywhere; you cannot be turned aside anywhere; you go with mastery everywhere. Therefore it is said:
"Letting go at the precipice, one personally accepts the responsibility. Only after death can one revive; then no one can deceive you.
If you can act thus, you may be said to be eternally still even as whirlwinds topple mountains. The river...
The rivers rush in competition yet do not flow; the wild horses of the desert gallop and flutter yet do not move; the sun and moon adorn the heavens yet do not circumambulate.
If this were not so, one would only perceive events passing before one’s eyes, unaware that old age creeps upon one from above.
Ascending the seat on New Year’s Day: Righteous Qi returns with the spring. The Lord of the East fans all things; within the realm of non-arising, he gives birth to the myriad existents.
Upon the foundation of non-abiding, he establishes all conditions. Sentient and insentient beings alike receive his transformative power.
Thus, outside the curtain of night-bright clarity, sovereign and subject celebrate at this moment; before the cliff of the withered tree, father and son shout for joy on this day.
"Virtuous practitioners of dhyāna, as for the gate of the rustic old man, how is it further? After a long silence, he said: 'Do you understand yet?
Son and grandson both possess the strength; within the room, one knows not of spring.'"
Ascending the hall, he held up his whisk and said: "When Da Hong’s whisk is raised, the spring light is lovely and the myriad trees harbor their fragrance;
when it is lowered, not a blade of grass grows, and all under heaven is of one color. Even though it is thus, if you observe closely, it is still merely the nest of worldly people.
How can one tread upon these two paths? After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand?"
"Only when the spring breeze is mild and warm will the flowers naturally bloom in the shade.
The Master, ascending the hall at Tianning Wanshou Chan Temple, offered incense and said:

"I humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, may share the longevity of Heaven and Earth, giving birth to and sustaining all things through non-action, and that you may shine with the brilliance of the Three Luminaries."

Illuminating the ten directions without interruption, he then ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying: "The three virtues unfold together to form pure conditions; the Sangha of the ten directions is the world’s fertile field."
I vow that through the merit of this day of non-action, may the imperial domain endure for ten million years.

Thus, in the luminous Lapis Lazuli Hall, sovereign and minister unite as one, their breaths merging like branches of the same tree; in the deep Moonlight Hall, father and son meet, sharing the same body and the same life-force.
As they walk together, the jade steps are covered in thick, mossy green; as they return hand in hand, the azure peaks and white clouds unfold before them.

Clouds swirl and wind around; throughout the entire body and to its very limits, there is nothing that does not accord with the occasion. Taking a step forward or turning back on the path, there is no other way. Therefore, from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one is always within it. Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether moving or still, one never departs from this very place.
Do you all understand? Throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm other than this. The four seas sing in joy as they offer their tribute.
One person: On this day, taking advantage of the extraordinary occasion of the Great Assembly for the Elevation of Prajñāpāramitā, I respectfully offer these merits to His Majesty the Emperor.
I humbly pray that his Way may equal that of the Five Emperors and his blessings surpass those of the heavens;
that his station may be as exalted as the North Star and his longevity as firm as Mount Nan-shan. Next, I pray for the Governor, the Vice-Governor, and the Prefectural and County Magistrates.

The civil and military officials and worthy associates have, through their virtue, dispelled the ailments of the people. Their reputation spread the awe that drives away wild beasts; their talent entered the Sage’s eyes. Their dream responded to the omen of the non-bear.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Excellent, all you practitioners of Zen! As sons of the Tathāgata, each of you should take the Way as your primary task. Directly—
One must cleanse the sense faculties and their objects, thereby purifying the three karmas.

Only when one’s every thought is undeviating within perfect, luminous right mindfulness can one enter the Way and escape birth and death. If this is not yet the case, you will merely don the rags of empty flowers and lose your mother-born trousers;
on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, you will find yourself flustered and frantic. I urge all you practitioners of Chan: once you have attained the seat...

Turning back to look within himself, he ascended the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat and said: "For three months of the summer retreat, we take Great Perfect Enlightenment as our monastery, with True Reality as its presiding master.
For ninety days of 'binding the feet,' we possess the wisdom of equality to protect all beings, tread the path, and benefit sentient beings. Although it is thus..."
Furthermore, you must know that there is one person who does not dwell in the observance of retreat, nor tread the path of protecting life.
Do you all recognize him? If you have not yet realized this, I cannot help but proclaim it once more: from time immemorial, neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs have been able to manage him.
The bright moon fills his head as he goes and returns; though the six gates have no acquaintances, how could there ever have been any confusion throughout antiquity and the present?

He gave this small discourse (*xiao can*) to the assembly, saying: "Excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners! The Dharma is fundamentally non-abiding, perfected wherever it is encountered. The Way transcends words."

Commentary: Established according to the capacity of the audience, the practitioners of the patch-robed school sometimes stand atop the highest mountain peaks, traversing freely through past and present;
sometimes they walk upon the deepest ocean floor, taking steps that completely transcend all, without peer.
Although it is thus, if one observes closely, it is still merely a matter of investigating principle.

But tell me, what is the phrase that transcends this? After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? When stillness reaches its limit, light penetrates; the fundamental is wondrous and perfect. A jade horse neighing in the wind passes through the heavy barrier.
Returning to the path, one does not fall into the age of Vimalacitra; the full power of wondrous function is seen beyond the teachings."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Dahong has this shadowless staff; with its tiger-squat and dragon-coil, who would dare approach it?
Sometimes held crosswise as he sits in the empty hall, even Linji and Deshan would lose their mettle.
Although it is so, tell me: where does its power lie? Do you all understand? It is most excellent when the moonlight spreads across the mossy steps; together we shall..."
Strolling leisurely about the Jade Hall, he ascended the hall and said:
"Half of the three-month summer retreat has already passed; as for this luminous ground of mind, how is it? Where there is seeking, there is inevitably the artifice of the intellect;
only when there is non-action can one truly avoid excessive calculation. Within the brazier, cold ashes waft with fragrant incense; before the crag..."
Withered trees and leaves flourish; a white-haired man atop a thousand peaks sings a new song of Xinfeng.
O practitioners of Zen, do you hear it? Its numinous ancient melody has never been interrupted; those who listen must understand it before any sign appears.
Ascending the hall, he held up his whisk and showed it to the assembly, saying: "The whisk of Da Hong has neither name nor lack of name;
before the seven Buddhas, it was fundamentally formed as one whole. It has neither form nor lack of form; it is profound yet bottomless, high yet unsurpassed.

If we discuss the time before yin and yang have manifested, both its rolling up and its unfolding are contained within the Treasury of Radiance. All you practitioners of Zen, how will you deal with this?"
"This is the Treasury of Radiance. Do you understand? It is vast and boundless, without any differentiated colors;

it illuminates all that has been and all that is yet to come. He ascended the hall and said: "Excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners! Within the realm of green jade there is no change or alteration; upon the ground of empty luminosity there is transcendence and subtlety.
How can one speak of this single phrase of wondrous perfection? Hidden and manifest, containing and merging—how could this be mistaken? At this point, for now, what shall you do?"
"What is the point where there is no error? Do you understand? The iron ox plows through the distant *hútiān*; though grand functions arise in abundance, they do not meet the occasion.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "For nine years at Shaolin, he offered but a single word; it has spread throughout all quarters, causing many to be misled by its recitation. Today, Dahong..."
With a wife’s heart, I cannot help but explain it clearly and in detail. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? The Lady of the Moon is clever;
she threads the golden needle through the broken silk. At midnight she embroiders the mandarin ducks—how many people can truly see her?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; has the wondrous form’s perfect luminosity been realized?

The clay Buddha does not pass through the water; the vast, resonant voice is beautiful beyond measure. The wooden Buddha does not pass through the fire; the ancient hall stands solitary, free of locks.
Herein, you must let go completely and return directly home; do not linger in vain halfway along the road. All you practitioners of Zen, how will you proceed?"

This is the matter of returning home. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? Sitting alone upon the root of a withered stone, the four oceans are waveless and the lunar disc stands solitary."
Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Heavenly Peace Festival (Tiānníngjié), he said: "The noble and extraordinary nature is inherently beyond the realm of effort and achievement;

it wondrously responds to the auspicious era while remaining unmanifest before the world. Therefore, within the Haoyin Hall, the Dharma drum is struck to expound the true mechanism; in the Vairocana Hall, the whale-bell is tolled to proclaim the ultimate principle.
Thus, the wind of Yao’s virtue fans far and wide, and the sun of Shun’s brilliance shines with clarity, as the myriad states offer congratulations upon his birth."
On this auspicious day for the Sage, the myriad nations offer prayers for the longevity of the Southern Mountain. But tell me, how many years of his life-span are there? Do you understand?
A single bright moon rises upon the sea’s surface; a jade-like person, casting off their shadow, counts the golden sands.
At Kōzan, he ascended the hall and said: "Before the Seven Buddhas, the vast road stretches far; within the realm of blue lapis lazuli, the moon’s brilliance is locked.
Donning robes and stepping through the door, the night grows ever deeper; casting off the hand and returning home, the sun has not yet slanted.

"O Zen practitioners, tell me: how would you express the single phrase of 'arriving home'? After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? Having traveled the path through the white clouds, [all is] still."

Hearing the sound of flowing water, he offered his thanks to the presiding seat and ascended the hall, saying: "The handle of the ladle and the strainer are held in one's own hands; letting go or holding fast is not a mere trap.
The morning and evening meals depend on single-minded devotion; the merit of benefiting oneself and others is imperishable. But how is it so?"
"The immortal achievement—do you understand? You must know that every grain of rice in the bowl was obtained through bitter toil.
He then addressed the supervisor of the monastery from the high seat, saying: "In the perfectly clear ocean of awakening, one may sport at will, yet a single hand cannot produce a sound.

On the bottomless boat of *utpala* flowers, we must all exert our strength together to ply the oars. Thus, those lost at the ferry crossing reach the shore, and those stalled in the waters forget their sorrows."
Nevertheless, even though it is thus, you must further know that there is one person who leaves no tracks when exiting a door and does not occupy the hall when entering a room;
all the sages who have arisen are merely messengers delivering words, and how could the various patriarchs who descended into the world ever dare to look upon them with their true eye?
Tell me, who is this person? Do you recognize him? Last night he happened to follow the flowing stream;
this morning he follows the white clouds back home.

Entering the hall, he said: "Profoundly still and without change, empty and penetrating with spiritual resonance—at the point where the wondrous function is exhausted and effort forgotten, all returns to..."
In the midst of stillness and illumination, he held up his whisk and said: "This is the whisk. Now tell me, which is the stillness?
Which is the illumination? Do you understand? A crane and a heron sleep side by side, treading the snow; startled by the bright moon, they both hesitate."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The late winter is piercingly cold; when a drop of water falls, it instantly forms a ball of ice. I recall the Patriarch of Shaolin, who stood knee-deep in snow—a hardship indeed.
Someone once said, 'I will settle your mind for you,' yet when one seeks the mind, not even a hair’s tip is to be found.

Suddenly, one remembers the path by which one came; in an instant, one realizes that the scene within the flask is vast and open. Within the light of lapis lazuli, everything is exactly as it is. At midnight...
The moon hangs low, perfectly full. [Zongmi] said: "The first three sons obtained the skin and flesh; the last one obtained the marrow and returned.
[Zongmi] said: "I do not ask about the first three sons. But tell me, who is that last one? Do you understand?
Viewed from afar, it is like a half-moon; viewed up close, it is like a hook. If you are one who knows the sound, contemplate this and nod your head in the dark."
For the rite of lighting the funeral pyre for a deceased monk, it is said: The great earth is blanketed in vast snow; a single phrase at the moment of departure is difficult to grasp.
The mud ox sinks into the immense deluge; the jade horse is cold amidst the flames.

If you can fully comprehend this point, you may truly be said to come like the moon dividing the myriad waters, and depart like clouds dispersing across a thousand peaks. If this is not yet so, I humbly pray that you will continue to strive toward it.

When performing the rite of lighting the funeral pyre for a deceased monk, it is said: "Through the harmony of the three conditions, existence is formed; when the four elements disperse, one returns to emptiness.
Now tell me, which among these is the true master, the presiding seat? Do you understand? When coming, there was no dependence; when going, what support is there?"
Red flames stretch across the sky, yet they never burn him.

This is said regarding the cremation of a deceased monk: "The renunciant has no leisure; all day long he busies himself in vain construction. At the moment of departure, his final concern is far too trivial.
Seeing with his eyes and hearing with his ears, why does he not fear? His hundred limbs lie in disarray—what was the point of it all?"
"Everyone is being asked to gather firewood for cremation. But tell me, among this, is there anything that burns yet does not dissolve?
All you Zen practitioners, the white clouds drift through the sky; vast, pure, and void, without a single crack."—Shangxiang.
True Praise for Chan Master Tianran, the Founder of Danxia:
The moon is cold over Mount Dan; the breeze is pure within the Patriarch’s chamber. Behold him, look up to him; his fame shall resound for a thousand years. The ancient Buddha does not remain.
The Sandalwood Buddha Image. Once, in a cold cliff, it was permitted that an iron ox would plow.
At Danxia, the second-generation Master Wuxue, the bright moon flows with radiance;
its reflection clarifies the cold waters. The myriad phenomena manifest together, and the great void is vast and open. The meditation board has already been repaid.
Of the highest caliber. When facing the challenge, he has not yet presented the meaning of the West’s coming.
Master An, the third generation of Danxia—his dragon-nose is neither high nor low;
his tiger-chin is neither short nor long. At midnight, the Kunlun child holds a silver bowl with both hands.
Chan Master Xun, the fourth generation descendant of Danxia, stood amidst a piercing, chilling wind.
His ancient countenance was majestic and imposing; he was the sun at its zenith in the continent of Kuru, yet the midnight hour in Jambudvīpa.
As for that single phrase prior to sound, let us deliberate upon it together.
Master Jingyin is true yet not truly so;
he is false yet not falsely so. Before the path of speech is set forth, his words fill the world.
A jade dragon lies coiled in the sea amidst deep, colored clouds; a black-lacquered Kunlun rides a jade horse.
In years past, the Elder of Banyang’s countenance was like jade; today, his hair is like frost. He no longer wears the golden robe, but instead dons white woolen garments.
A multicolored phoenix perches at night upon a tree without shadow; in the dawn sky, clouds part to reveal the slanting sun.
A Zen practitioner has painted a portrait of the Master and requested a eulogy.
*Tut!* This withered and emaciated form has, throughout his life, been far too bold in exposing the heavens. It is the mechanism of lightning and sparks—a matter of two-tongued [sharp] discernment.
Returning alone, he has no mouth; cutting straight to the root, he refuses to speak. He loves to lead his Zen followers wandering through the wild weeds.
The real is not real, and the false is not false. With round eyes and brows arched, with ugly lips and a flat nose—how difficult it is to capture this in a painting;
where can one find it through mere thought? The moon enfolds the treetops as the crane’s dream first awakens; snow covers the reeds as the heron shivers in the cold.
Do not sleep;
paint out the form of the illness so that the eyebrows and eyes are distinct. Even if it were entirely like the original, you would only achieve eighty percent.
To hear the name is not as good as seeing the face; to see the face is not as good as hearing the name. When the moon fills the frosty sky, it is difficult to find the old hare; at the sea...
The tide has receded from the gate; one seeks not the long whale.
Verses on the Five Ranks.
In the midst of the upright, there is partiality: the precious palace is shrouded in mist before the moonlight. A lamp is lit at the bottom of the well while heaven has not yet dawned;
in the darkness, who can distinguish the source from its destination?

In partiality, there is the midst of the upright: Mǔmǔ stands before her makeup, ashamed to look into the mirror. At the third watch, the jade doors are not lit by lamps; they blend and merge, beyond [duality].
The shadow of years is revealed.
Coming from the center, he strides through the red furnace across the nine realms. The precious moon’s night-light is tranquil wherever it falls;
though it parts the clouds, not even a speck of dust is exposed.
Reaching the ultimate within the partial: when great function is impartial, how can it be deliberated? Facing the front, how could one be willing to fall into the present age?

His house possesses a transcendent will of its own. Reaching the ultimate within the simultaneous: exhausting existence and non-existence is truly wondrous. Wearing fur and horns, walking through fire—transverse and vertical, there is no obstruction.
Falling into the path of the present age;

furthermore, this is "the partial within the central. When the light of the jewel moon congeals in the sky above the ocean floor, why is it that the fisherman’s boat can never be fully laden? The radiance flows and competes.
Willingly penetrating the waves, one is centered within the partiality;
deep waters and clouds lock away the fisherman’s dwelling. A single current flows through the long river, its clarity extending to the horizon.
When the sun shines upon the bamboo pole, how could its shadow remain hidden?

Coming from the very center: A light single-leaf boat drifts upon the distant shoals. Since the scarlet-scaled fish do not touch the fragrant hook or bait, why should the line and cord further offend with its scent?
Arriving from within the partiality: Drawing in the line, he returns once more to the reeds; leaning high upon his tortoise-pillow, he sleeps at ease as he pleases. The Long River flows on in trust.
Let the waves rise as they will;
he arrives simultaneously within the midst of them. As the night draws to a close, there is no news from the six dwellings; he wanders freely and at ease upon the roads of the marshy realm.
For a woodcutter, it would be difficult even to set foot there.
Dwelling in seclusion on my return journey, the jade horse need no longer accompany me; behind the horns of the earthen ox, do not lay the whip.
Thankful for the Great Universe’s sustaining embrace, I sleep at ease amidst the drifting clouds and fragrant grasses, following my own nature.

In our own school, the empty kalpa is self-existent, with nothing to rely upon or maintain. Since time immemorial, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have found it difficult to open their mouths. For nine years he faced the wall—there was already too much fuss;
how much more so to insist on distinguishing between the beautiful and the ugly?
The fisherman stands by the sea’s edge as the smoke clears and evening falls; his light skiff glides out from the reed cove.
Casting his line into the clear waves at night, he catches a golden-scaled fish at dawn that has not even touched the pole.
A Letter Sent with Master Sheng to Convey the Dharma Lineage:
Fluttering petals in the warm sun send you off lightly; The blazing flames must be penetrated by a true adept. Meeting face-to-face, there is no need for the path of words;
Across a thousand li of Vermilion Mountain, we share the same wind.
Seeing off my Dharma brother, the Head Seat Ying:
Falling leaves drift thickly as ten thousand plants wither; His cloud-robes lightly unfurled, he descends from the high peaks.
In years to come, when the flowers and branches stir in glory, The rootless sacred tree will grow its sprouts in secret.
Seeing off Master Jing:
Originally perfected from the start, it does not depend on words. A clay ox plows the fields of the primordial kalpa. At night, the wind and moon possess a heavy frost-like majesty;
at dawn, Kunlun returns wearing snow upon his head.
In response to the words of the man of the Way, Jiji:
Before the word, there is no phrase; how could one attempt to extend it? Wondrous speech and profound discourse are but dust in the eye.
The assembly at Vaiśālī, like golden grains, will surely turn their laughter upon this mountain-dweller.
The moon is bright over the seamless stupa; auspicious vapors swirl around the fishing boat. Amidst the deep reeds, the night tides are cold. How pitiable are those who cast their lines endlessly;
following the crowd in their frantic haste, they lose their fishing rods.
The story of Zhaozhou’s old woman exposing the truth;
the wooden man sings atop the ridge, the stone woman dances by the stream. The bright moon shares a single path, its impartial light illuminating past and present.
By Master He Jingyin, in the style of *Yufu Ci*:
With no home in the four seas, what constraints can bind me? I sit casting my line, facing misty clouds and vapors. The waters are swift and the breeze gentle;
my boat glides with ease. The severe frost approaches. My lotus robes, bamboo hat, and reed screen are all worn like mist.

The great-scaled fish always hides within the deep currents; today it has been caught on the hook—truly strange! As the oars strike the waves and the surging tides, the mulberry fields are transformed.
The three calamities have destroyed all; only then can one say that one’s livelihood truly endures.
The decrepit old fisherman has no understanding at all. With his gray, snow-white hair, who knows how many years he has spent? With a short oar and a light boat, he drifts upon the vast blue sea.
He casts his hook; in the depths of the azure waves, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
The scaled dragon swallows the bait and stirs the floating line; the woodcutters on both banks all cherish it. It passes straight through the Dragon Gate, its head and horns transformed.
Who could find fault? Only when it brings forth rain does it manifest its great spiritual penetration.
Sending off Elder Sheng to reside at Dacheng:
The bright moon flows its radiance, chilling the thousand peaks; the clay ox walks slowly out from the clouds and mist.
If seekers of the profound ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey, point directly to the time before the womb was formed.
Seeing off Pu Junsu as he departs for his post as Judicial Commissioner of Hunan, I carry my staff and wipe away my sweat as I bid farewell to the literary star.
A pure breeze sweeps across the land, towering over a hundred cities. He cannot remain within the ranks of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
green moss grows upon the crystal palace.
I bid farewell to Old Lady Pang:
in every land is the meaning of the West, in every speck of dust is the heart of the ancient Buddhas. Her eyebrows serve as dharma companions;
her nostrils act as intimate friends. I ask where Niutou has gone—where can the flower-bearing, hidden birds be found?

Before Assistant Lecturer Ji arrived at Vaiśālī to practice his medical arts, he did not yet know of Vimalakīrti’s illness. There is a guest, a skilled physician whose wondrous art penetrates the divine and the sacred;
with a golden needle, he brings forth the "Skull's Lament. For a thousand years, who could rival this melody?
In response to Secretary Liu Chaofeng, two verses:
The lines that give strength to one’s life have all been spoken by Vimalakīrti. A single flask of heaven within the empty kalpa; the clay ox plows through the moon.
Appearing in the guise of an official, he is unrecognized by men; his mind dwells in the ancestral realm, nourished by the essence of the Way.
He does not prize the golden seal as large as a bushel, but cherishes the priceless jewel within his own robe.
Seeing Master Junchua Return Home to Beg for a Mat:
In years past, Baizhang once lightly rolled it up; Today he returns again to his native land to seek it.
Suddenly, within the three months of summer heat in the Cloud Hall, He cries out to Heaven as it abruptly turns to a clear autumn.
In response to Master Man:
Do not say that silence is wondrous. How could he who faced the wall ever have failed to speak? Reflecting back on the Golden-Colored Dhūta, he instead pushed over the flagpole.
The Fisherman Father and Son escort the two transformation-masters, Qi and Ming;
a piercing, solemn wind chills to the very bone. A light skiff glides gently over the azure waves. The golden line is straight; the jade hook is poised.
Countless scaled fish leap and frolic upon the emerald bamboo;
the fisherman’s nature has always been broad and easygoing. Though he catches a full boat, it is not yet cause for joy. Having finished reeling in his line, he gazes toward the layered peaks.
Raising my head, I realize for the first time that dawn has broken and the stars at the edge of the sky are fading.
Governor Xie and Scholar Zhang have bestowed upon me a fine woolen rug;

in this empty chamber, it is even deeper and colder, and I cannot sleep. Sitting alone in solitude for many years, the sound of the wind whistles past. Last night, once again, I found myself lingering in meditation.
Sleeping, it is as if upon a newly spread mat of white jade.
In winter, a monk stays in his mountain hut;
fallen leaves accumulate over the moss. The wooden gate is half-unopened. The secluded forest is densely covered by clouds; flowers and birds come in vain, filled with regret.
Seeing Wang Rubi, the Teacher of the Way,
his worldly livelihood entirely exhausted; with not even a needle’s point of land left to bequeath to his descendants, he cast off his hands and departed for the green peaks,
returning with effortless ease to the village of white clouds.

Sending forth the transformation-monk, the spring clouds possess no worldly sentiment; their nourishing moisture arises and spreads everywhere. Following the dragon, they fly toward the sea and disperse as rain upon the world.
In the secluded caverns, where there are no gates, they may roll up or unfurl at will; do not forget the father of the green mountains in your long journey.
Five Poems in the Style of the Fisherman’s Song With white hair, the old fisherman discusses the end of the year. How many times has the mulberry field changed, yet you remain ever-present.
On the banks of red smartweed, in the villages of reed flowers—the water and moon are empty and bright, leaving no trace of duality.
Lifting my eyes, who is there to meet me? Nothing can be grasped. In tranquil solitude, I face alone the water and clouds at rest.
Amidst mountain colors and between billowing waves, the wondrous body stands majestic, its countenance unrevealed.
The azure void serves as both line and hook; the broken rope is a basket, a boat without a bottom.
Floating freely, drifting with the currents, one finds liberation amidst the surging jade waves.
Lightly gliding the fragrant boat to the edge of the sea, cast the hook and let down the line without hesitation.
O young dragon, O great turtle—unharmed by the clear waves, you shall be caught on the line.

Having fished the rivers and lakes until dawn, the morning light divides. A few notes of the *qiang* flute carry their melody beyond the clouds. The waves are vast and boundless; the mists are thick and swirling.
Beating the oars and turning the boat, one gazes toward the edge of the sea.
In Praise of Tending the Ox by Layman Wujin:
Before its horns and head have even emerged, it sleeps soundly amidst the deep, swirling clouds. It does not follow the fragrant grasses away toward the distant mountains;
what need is there for the boy with the straw hat to apply the whip?
In response to Chan Master Min-feng’s illumination of this matter, he showed it through a verse:
The waters are broad and the clouds deep; the ancient path is far. The Chan companions of the Five Lakes share a common home. Last night, I joyfully received a true message:
In the forest of no shadows, the rotten wood blooms with flowers.
Entrusting my elder brother, the Dharma friend Jizhao:
his body contains the void before any sign arises. How could he, in such carefree ease, dwell as a neighbor to things? Let the wind, moon, frost, and heavy rigors pass as they may;
like flowers on a withered tree, he does not violate the spring.
I visited the Preceptor of the Monastery at Moyao Hall but did not meet him;
the edict of Magadha from years past—today who would recognize its grace? Beyond the phrase, one contemplates the hidden essence; prior to words, one discusses the secret intent.
The pines and wind purify the universe; the cassia moon illuminates heaven and earth. Though one may not go out the door, how can this compare to quietly closing it?
Master Jing has fallen ill and sent me this verse:
"Fire, wind, earth, and water combine to form the body, like a single speck of dust in the clear sky. I ask you, from where does this illness arise?"
Arise! Who, indeed, is the one who is ill?
Retiring from his post, he showed two verses to the two Chan practitioners, Yu and Huan;
for ten years they together upheld the fundamental principles. The myriad kinds of contradictions were all known to them, yet today there is not a single one that remains.

The matter is this: sitting and watching the bright moon shine upon the lapis lazuli, the water is most clear and the moon is most full. Moonlight contains the water, and the water reflects the sky; they blend and merge, falling not into the world of Vimalacitra.
Reaching this point, how can one speak of the orthodox or the biased?
Sending off Huán the Guest Attendant to Return Home to Visit His Parents:
"Clear breezes and bright moonlight—autumn light fills half the sky. Chan Master Huán took his leave of me, saying he was returning south.

On the day mother and child meet within the hall, Who would dare to separate their wondrous perfection? Eh! Turning over the upward-moving pivot of my house, Turning one's head, it is touched everywhere.
A radiance is born.

Before the signs appear when the Master Jue sends forth his wondrous transformation among different species, his lofty head and horns tower toward the heavens. On your return journey, do not linger by the cold shore.
Grass. Plowing through the fields beyond the limit of Vipaśyin.
Thank you, King, for your visit and the transmission of the teaching;
my thatched gate always stands open facing the white clouds. The jade phoenix carries the flower away and returns again. I do not follow the distant example of Donglin.
Wine. Yuanming offers many thanks for your visit to the mountains.
I rejoice that Master Gongyu of Wuyun has come to pay a visit;

on this mountain path, the spring breeze carries the fragrance of peach and plum blossoms. The elder of Yanling has graced my mountain retreat. As you walk along, may you be vast and open, forgetting the way.
Every step is serene, merging with the site of enlightenment; the wondrous and pure vehicle of the ultimate teaching is like cranes roosting in pines.
The field of empty clarity holds frost within its moonlight. When we meet and encounter one another, what is there to do? We converse of the light behind the crown of Vairocana.
The Chan practitioner who contemplates stillness as a mendicant, returning to the source like an infant, transcends ten thousand years in a single thought; he knows nothing of spring or autumn.
The shadowless tree on the cold cliff has been hewn down; turning one's head, it sprouts branches once more within the flames. When spring has faded, he departs from me to enter the marketplace;
when conditions arise, there will surely be a return to the mountains—*ei!* Sitting together, we gaze at the clean mat; a pure breeze rises from the four quarters.

The Harmony and Right Knowledge Treasury, the Shixuan Hall—this newly opened space is not for ornate decoration. It is intended to cherish coolness and dispel the heat and dampness. From where do these myriad scenes come?
Not even a speck of dust can enter here. The meditation cushions and Zen boards are profoundly still; the resonance of pines and the breeze through the bamboos are ever-present.
Gong gong. The incense has faded and the burner is cold as I sit through the deep night. The moon fills the mossy courtyard, yet no one stands there.
Thank you, my good friend from Mengcheng, for your gift of rice;
when guests arrive at Mengcheng, I shall have news to send back. You have generously provided rice to assist with the morning cooking; the old monk’s bowl is full, and he is too weary to respond.
A call! The elder’s profound kindness is known only to himself; each grain is perfectly formed, difficult to comprehend. Clearly chewed to pieces, what further doubt remains?
Zhaozhou’s bequeathed words are truly not in error: once fully satiated, one naturally forgets a hundred hungers.

Entrusting this to my virtuous friend, I seek a verse on the difficult-to-traverse path of differentiation; one must surely recognize one's own school. Rootless withered tree-seeds cast layer upon layer of shadows under the moonlit night.
Danxia praises his dharma-brother for newly constructing a "Warm Hall," and celebrates it with this verse.

The newly constructed Warm Hall reaches toward the heights of the clouds; the cassia moon and pine winds ever fill its embrace. Amidst the radiance of the celestial lamps, it responds serenely to the times;
before words are spoken, the wondrous song proclaims the Way of Pan’yang.
**Five Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains** A thatched hut is built at the foot of the forest slopes; Tranquil and carefree, it serves as my dwelling. The pines and wind startle me from my dreams;

The mountain stream’s ice still reflects the void. In late spring, the flowers remain lovely; At the end of autumn, the leaves are not yet sparse. On these auspicious nights, with boundless sentiment, The moon rises over the eastern ridge.
This very field of leisure remains unchanged through all time; The mud ox plows it forevermore, and the precious moon is eternally full.
Rock-olives shimmer with misty green, and stream-flowers glisten fresh with dew. Content to dwell within the blue peaks, I am too weary to seek out the men of the age.

My home lies near the foot of chaotic mountains; when the sun is high, I am too weary to open the gate. Woodsmen’s songs resound beyond the clouds; the melodies of the Hu people are discussed before my very steps.
The path is so remote that no one ever arrives; the courtyard is overgrown, marked only by traces of moss. Amidst the rustling of crags and rocks, I simply grow old in this village of mist and smoke.
Sitting upright, I dwell in constant practice; who knows this state of mind? The breeze through the bamboo has a light melody; the mountain stream flows subtly without sound.

Lofty and majestic are the three peaks in their splendor; tender and lingering is the crescent moon’s clarity. Before my gate stands a withered tree; the solitary crane finds it hard to fulfill its dream.

No lingering attachment to the gates of white clouds; casting off all ties, one returns to the home mountain. The jade incense burner wafts fragrant smoke; the waters of the stone ravine flow with a murmuring sound.

Mist enshrouds the trees in the courtyard; raindrops paint patterns upon the windows and eaves. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one always dwells within the realm of stillness and solitude.
Sent to Official Shouxiang:
Three Poems In the cold of winter, I originally intended to grow old in the mountain forests; Now, bathed in the radiance of your grace, I enter the verdant heights.
Once again adjusting my hands that once cast the fishing line, I follow conditions by the Yun River, carefree and at ease.
The Way is one and has never been separated by so much as a hair’s breadth; those who part and yet meet again are rare indeed. Now, by chance, I have once more received your pure illumination;
the pine wind and cassia moon assail me with their chilling cold.
Upon the stringless zither lies the rare sound; this encounter with one who knows the music serves as witness. Without touching the fingertips, a single melody is played:
in the realm of azure lapis lazuli, the moon shines at the third watch.

Seeing Off Master Wu Gongyu: The weather is warm and bright, a spring day in the third month. Green mountains descend to visit this white-haired man. His demeanor is dignified and solemn as he reveals his refined elegance;

his discourse is clear and cool, washing away the dust of thirst. When the Way accords with the perfect and eternal, there is no divergent path; when the mind is empty, one has passed the imperial examination by oneself.
A common thoroughfare: meeting and parting, do not harbor lingering thoughts. Though a thousand *li* apart, we share the same breeze;
in virtue, we are neighbors. The Venerable Jian requested a verse:

In the nineteenth year, encountering the news of spring, The plum blossoms break through the snow and bloom. If you can understand this within, Then your journey from a thousand *li* has not been in vain.

In harmony with Layman Zhang Mumen, his realization is profound and his mind empty and luminous. The moon is pushed forth by the toad to illuminate the heart of heaven. Before the pine wind has begun, the cold forest is still;
he plays a single note of the soundless zither’s melody.
In response to what was sent by Zhang Bowei:

Today I have come once more to sit amidst the warm clouds. My old friend smiles and says my appearance is that of an elder. Within this emptiness of kalpas, there is yet another spring within the jar;
facing the green mountains amidst the clouds, my inspiration knows no bounds.
Two Poems Sent by Heshang Yangshu Do not test the water and milk with the king of geese;
There is another method for discerning the fine from the coarse. The original ground requires no power of springtime;
Beyond the kalpas, the numinous branches retain their lingering fragrance.
Shi Kuang and Li Lou were not my peers; with clarity, he who is beyond form obtained the dark pearl. When the mind sprouts and the mouth attempts to describe it, a track is formed;
yet how can this perfect luminosity be categorized as either existent or non-existent?
In response to Mr. Liu Yushu’s wondrous verse:
Spiritual resonance overflows the eyes with cold clarity; The subtle and profound meaning is difficult to encounter again. Meeting once more, we inquire further of the stringless lute;
The wind enters the pine branches—it is not played upon.
In the *Record of the Sayings of Chan Master Chun of Duhong Mountain in Suizhou*,

it is stated that the Way of Dongshan had been transmitted through six generations until it was on the verge of extinction at Dayang. Touzi continued the lineage, and after three further transmissions,
it reached [Master Chun].
Chan Master Danxia Chun emerged as one of the two sons of Zhenxie and Hongzhi to propagate their school’s teachings.
Viewed from this perspective, the Master was truly the restorer of our tradition. Nevertheless, the essential sayings of the Master have been lost to the world;
thus, his descendants have harbored regret for this deficiency. Recently, I happened to obtain the *Dharma-Transmission Record of the Thirteenth Generation*.
This was transcribed by Sun Dayong of Qinggong. This single volume of the Master’s *Recorded Sayings* from his residence at Da’hong is like encountering sweet rain on a parched day.
Beyond my joy and elation, I have raised funds to publish it so that its transmission may be broadened. Therefore, I have composed this verse to respectfully inscribe upon its back: [Verse omitted]
Overturning the waters of the cave, he spread the flourishing tradition; Vast waves and billows were sprinkled across the lands east of the sun.
Six hundred years have passed through frost, yet it has not perished; Re-engraved on woodblocks, may it flow forth forever.
The first ten days of the late spring in the seventh year of Baoying.
The distant descendant, the young bhikṣu Ryōki, having washed his hands and performed a hundred prostrations, records this supplement to the *Recorded Sayings of Zen Master Danxia Chun*.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form. (Zhao)
The Dharma Master speaks thus; he only knows how to point to tracks and discuss traces, yet he cannot pick it up and show it to others.
Today, Danxia tears open the universe and shatters the mountain of form to bring it forth for you all. Let those with eyes discern it!
He struck the ground once with his staff and said, "Do you see? 'The egret standing in the snow is not of the same color; the bright moon among the reeds is not like it.
He ascended the hall and cited Deshan’s address to the assembly, which said: "In my school there are no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Deshan...
When Shan speaks in this manner, it can be said that he only knows how to enter the grass to seek people, yet remains unaware that his entire body is covered in mud and water.
Upon careful observation, he possesses but a single eye. If it were Danxia, it would not be so: "In my school there is a saying:
'The golden scissors cannot cut it open; the profound and mysterious principle is the jade maiden conceiving in the night.'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Stately at midday, the sun is still half-hidden; Silent at the third watch, it has not yet reached fullness.
The six gates have never known the warmth of spring; Coming and going, they always remain before the third watch."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The precious moon flows with radiance; its reflection spreads across the clear pool. The water has no intention of soaking the moon; the moon has no mind to divide its light.
When both water and moon are forgotten, only then can it be called 'severance. Therefore it is said: 'The matter of ascending to heaven must be cast away;
the matter of ten-fold perfection must be discarded. When the golden sound is thrown to the ground, there is no need to look back. If you can be like this..."
It is so. At the very beginning of understanding, one enters among those of different kinds. Do you people here fully comprehend this? After a long silence, he said:
"Constantly walking without lifting the feet of the human stride; wearing fur and horns, mingling with the mud and dust."
As Zhenxie was in the midst of his training, the Master asked him, "What is your original self prior to the empty kalpa? Zhenxie prepared to answer, but the Master said, "You are making a fuss.

Go for now. One day, while atop Potu Peak, Zhenxie attained sudden enlightenment. He returned directly to stand in attendance upon the Master, who struck him with his palm and said, "I thought you knew;
it turns out you do. Zhenxie bowed joyfully. The following day, the Master ascended the hall and said, "The sun shines upon the solitary peak."
Cui: "The moon descends upon the mountain stream, cold. The profound and wondrous instructions of the Patriarch—do not settle them within a single inch of the mind. He then descended from his seat.
Xie stepped forward directly and said, "Today’s ascent of the seat cannot deceive me further. The Master said, "Try to cite for me what I said today as I ascended the seat.
After a long silence, the Master said, "I thought you had attained some sudden realization. Xie then departed.
When Hongzhi was attending the assembly, the Master asked, "What is your original self before the empty kalpa? Hongzhi replied, "A shrimp at the bottom of the well swallows the moon;
at the third watch, one does not borrow the light of the night-curtain. The Master said, "Not yet—speak further. Hongzhi hesitated.
The Master struck once with his whisk and said, "It is also called 'not borrowing. At these words, Zhi attained great enlightenment.
A monk asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master replied, "The golden chrysanthemums have just begun to bloom; bees vie to gather their pollen."
He asked, "What is it like after seeing? The Master said, "The sprouts wither and the flowers fall; there is nothing left to rely upon.
He cited an ancient precedent, citing how Bei-yuan asked Qing-feng about Luo-pu’s saying: "Entering a wasteland, one does not discriminate; one simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand. Why?
“Do not say so. What is this ‘grass plucked at random’? Feng made a gesture as if picking something up.
The Master said, “It is indeed so, yet you have not yet been able to eat the grass.”
When they raised the case of the practitioner Gan-zhi receiving guests, a monk said, "It is not easy for a practitioner to receive guests.

Gan-zhi replied, "It is like feeding a donkey or feeding a horse. Ming-an said, "I know that the practitioner constantly travels this path. The Master [Yun-men] spoke separately, saying, "Next year, I will buy a straight-cut robe (zhidu) for the practitioner."
In a verse-commentary on an ancient precedent, a monk asked Jiufeng Qian: "I have heard it said that you, Master, have remarked: 'The various sages who appear from time to time are merely messengers.
Is this true? The Master replied, "Yes. The monk continued, "When the World-Honored One pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward the earth, saying..."
"Throughout the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. Why did the Master [Nanquan] instead call him a "messenger"?
The Teacher said, "Precisely because he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, he was called a messenger."
The wondrous marks are perfectly luminous and cannot be grasped; the slaves and servants are merely diligent in their service.
Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, they claim to be honorable and great—yet they too are merely messengers transmitting words.
A monk asked Dōngshān Shuàn, "When it is said that a pure practitioner does not enter nirvana and a precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell, what is the case?
The Master said, "When all have been delivered without a trace remaining, he returns to transcend even nirvana."
With marks and signs so majestic, a great man indeed; in his whole life he was without "wisdom" and appeared just like a fool. From of old, even Buddhas and Patriarchs could hardly hope to reach him;
how could hell or heaven possibly constrain him?
When Chan Master Qingyuan Si first visited the Sixth Patriarch, he asked, "What should one attend to so as not to fall into stages?
The Patriarch replied, "What have you been doing? The Master said, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "In what stage would you then fall?
The Master said, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stage could there be? The Patriarch held him in high esteem.
Transcendent and solitary, it is difficult to peer into with the orthodox eye. Far surpassing past and present, its kind is hard to equal. Moss seals the ancient hall where no one serves;
the moon locks Cangwu, and the phoenix does not perch.
Qingyuan asked on account of a stone: "How long has it been since the Master left the mountain ridges? The Master said, "I do not know when you departed from Caoxi.
[Qingyuan] said, "Xiqian did not come from Caoxi. The Master said, "I also know where you have gone.
[Qingyuan] said, "Master, as you are a person of great stature, please do not speak so hastily."
A wooden man comes to inquire about the path to the azure heavens; the stone woman, being old, seems not to hear. Taking each other’s hands, they return together to their native land;
the evening mountains rise steeply, locked in heavy clouds.
One day, while Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyen was sitting on a rock, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here?
The Master replied, "I am doing nothing at all. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly.
The Master said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. Shitou asked, "Since you say you are doing nothing, then what exactly are you not doing? The Master replied:
Even a thousand sages do not recognize him. He praised him with a verse, saying: "From the beginning we have lived together, yet you did not know my name;

We have traveled along together by natural spontaneity, just as we were. Since antiquity, even the most eminent sages have failed to recognize him; How could ordinary people in their haste ever understand him?"

When the profound and subtle reach their ultimate limit, one is naturally serene. If you say there are eighteen thousand miles between us, the moon reflects upon the clear river and the fish do not see it;
why must the fisherman further cast away his trap?
Daowu was once asked by Shishuang, "If someone were to ask about the ultimate matter after a hundred years have passed, what would you say to him?
The Master called to a novice; the novice responded, "Yes. The Master said, "Add some water to the pure pitcher.

After a long silence, the Master then asked Shishuang, "What was it you were asking just now? As Shishuang was about to repeat his question, the Master immediately returned to his quarters. At this, Shishuang attained realization.
There is realization.
Extending his hand, he returns the author’s pivot; within ordinary speech, he arrays the spear and banner. Repeatedly questioning and about to advance, he returns to the abbot’s quarters;
one phrase is clear, and there is no further doubt.
When Daowu arrived at Wufeng, Wufeng asked him, "Do you recognize the old master Yaoshan? The Master said, "I do not recognize him.
Wufeng asked, "Why do you not recognize him? The Master said, "I do not recognize him; I do not recognize him."
Where white clouds dwell in depths, the path is difficult to traverse; to seek its traces is already to involve effort. The wild goat hanging from a cliff leaves no trace;
yet even in such composure, one still falls into the midst of the direct and the biased.
Yunyan, my fellow practitioner, I returned from Nanquan to Yaoshan. I asked Yaoshan, "What is it like to walk among those of different species?
Yaoshan said, "I am weary today; wait until another time to come. I replied, "I have come to the mountain specifically for this matter.
Yaoshan said, "Go for now. I then departed. I was at that time in the abbot’s quarters.
Hearing from outside that the Master had not recommended him, he unconsciously bit his finger until it bled.
Coming down, he asked the Master, "Brother, you went to ask the Abbot; what was the outcome? The Master said, "He would not speak for me.
Thereupon, [the other] bowed his head.
When hungry, he eats tender grass as he wanders through distant mountains; when thirsty, he drinks cold spring water as he turns back from winding ravines.
Roaming freely upon the empty lands of the kalpa before creation, what need is there for the evening sky to urge him on with the sound of herding songs?
Yunyan was once asked by a monk, "For twenty years you served Baizhang as his attendant, providing him with his handkerchief and ewer;
why was the lamp of your mind not transmitted? Yunyan said, "The precious flower crown upon my head. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the precious flower crown upon my head'?"
The Master said, "The Emperor of the Great Tang and the King of the Netherworld.

Later, a monk raised this question with Chan Master Jiugong Qian, asking, "What is the meaning of 'the Emperor of the Great Tang and the King of the Netherworld'? Qian replied, "I recall the words of Dongshan."
The jade whip is raised high to strike the golden gate; it draws forth the coral whose value is beyond reckoning. The ancient Wheel-Turning King fully manifests his spirit and vigor;
without displaying the precious seal, he is naturally honored.
The novice Gao was staying in a hermitage. One day, he came through the rain to visit Yaoshan.
Yaoshan said, "You have come. The master replied, "I have. Yaoshan said, "It is quite soaked. The master said, "This does not strike the drum or the flute.
Yunyan said, "There is not even skin; what drum could one strike? Daowu said, "There is not even a drum; what skin could one strike? The master said, "Now..."
What a magnificent performance on this fine day!
